prompt: Which tile below completes the wall next to it?

solutions.title: Match the corners
solutions.body:
Where four tiles meet, their corners make one of two patterns: a **full dark circle** (four quarter-circles) or a **dark star** (four spikes and pointed shapes).

Look at the four corners of the gap:
- top-right corner: it is part of a dark circle → the new tile needs a **quarter-circle** there;
- top-left and bottom-right corners: they are part of stars → the new tile needs **spikes** there;
- bottom-left corner: a plain rounded pink corner.

Tile (E) has exactly one quarter-circle, two spikes and one rounded corner in this order around the tile. Turned a quarter turn clockwise, its quarter-circle goes to the top-right and the spikes go to the top-left and bottom-right — it fits.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
The gap needs one quarter-circle, two spikes and one plain rounded corner.
- (A) has three spikes and no plain rounded corner ✗
- (B) has two quarter-circles ✗
- (C) has no quarter-circle ✗
- (D) has no spikes ✗

Only (E) has the right corners (it just has to be turned a quarter turn).

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: Amira is travelling from Atown to Betown and passes two signposts along the road. One of them has a hidden number. What is this number?

solutions.title: Find the whole distance
solutions.body:
At the first sign, Atown is 2 km behind and Betown is 9 km ahead. So the whole road is $2 + 9 = 11$ km.

At the second sign, Betown is 4 km ahead, so Atown is $11 - 4 = 7$ km behind.

**Answer: (C) 7**

solutions.title: Count how far she drove
solutions.body:
From the first sign to the second, the distance to Betown went down from 9 km to 4 km, so Amira drove $9 - 4 = 5$ km.

That means the distance from Atown went **up** by 5 km: $2 + 5 = 7$ km.

**Answer: (C) 7**

prompt: The board shown is made of small white and dark squares. After a quarter turn (90 degrees), what can the board look like?

solutions.title: Turn it column by column
solutions.body:
When you turn the board a quarter turn **clockwise**, each column (read from bottom to top) becomes a row (read from left to right).

Original board (D = dark, W = white):
- row 1: D W D W
- row 2: W D D W
- row 3: D D W D
- row 4: D W W D

Turned clockwise, the new rows are:
- D D W D
- W D D W
- W W D D
- D D W W

That is board (D).

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Follow one special square
solutions.body:
Look at the original top row: D W D W. After a clockwise quarter turn, the top row moves to the **right-hand column**, reading top to bottom: D, W, D, W.

Check the right-hand column of each choice: only (D) reads dark, white, dark, white from top to bottom. A quick check of another row confirms it.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Ana lights a new candle every 10 minutes. Each candle burns for 40 minutes. After 55 minutes, how many candles will be lit?

solutions.title: Make a timeline
solutions.body:
Candles are lit at minutes 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. Each burns for 40 minutes:
- lit at 0 → out at 40 ✗
- lit at 10 → out at 50 ✗
- lit at 20 → out at 60 ✓
- lit at 30 → out at 70 ✓
- lit at 40 → out at 80 ✓
- lit at 50 → out at 90 ✓

At minute 55, 4 candles are burning.

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: Look back 40 minutes
solutions.body:
A candle is still burning at minute 55 if it was lit during the last 40 minutes, i.e. after minute 15. The candles lit after minute 15 are those at 20, 30, 40 and 50 → 4 candles.

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: When the card is flipped over its top edge, we see the photo of the kangaroo shown. If instead we flip the card over its right edge, what will we see?

solutions.title: Two flips differ by a half turn
solutions.body:
Flipping over the top edge and flipping over the right edge show the same back of the card, but the two pictures are turned **upside down** compared with each other (a half turn).

In the top-flip picture, the skateboard is at the top, the head is at the bottom and the tail points left. Turning it a half turn: skateboard at the bottom, head at the top, tail pointing **right**. That is picture (D).

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Try it with a card
solutions.body:
Draw an arrow pointing up on the back of a card. Flip it over the top edge: the arrow points down. Flip it (from the start) over the right edge: the arrow points up. So the two views are upside down compared with each other.

Turn the kangaroo picture upside down: the head goes up and the tail points right → (D). (A) is a mirror image, not a half turn.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Bia has the five coins shown: 1 real, 50 centavos, 25 centavos, 10 centavos and 5 centavos. She goes to the grocery store to buy a piece of fruit using exactly three coins, without receiving change. Which of the following prices can she **not** pay?

solutions.title: Make each price
solutions.body:
All prices are more than 1 real, and the four small coins add up to only 90 centavos, so the 1-real coin is always used. The other two coins must make the rest:
- 1.30: 25 + 5 ✓
- 1.35: 25 + 10 ✓
- 1.40: need 40 from two of 50, 25, 10, 5 — the pairs give 75, 60, 55, 35, 30, 15. No 40 ✗
- 1.55: 50 + 5 ✓
- 1.75: 50 + 25 ✓

**Answer: (C) 1.40 reais**

solutions.title: List all two-coin sums
solutions.body:
With the 1-real coin plus two others, the possible totals are:

$1 + \{50+25, 50+10, 50+5, 25+10, 25+5, 10+5\}$ = 1.75, 1.60, 1.55, 1.35, 1.30, 1.15 reais.

1.40 is not on the list.

**Answer: (C) 1.40 reais**

prompt: In a garden, a bush has branches with seven leaves, or branches with four leaves and a flower. Janaina counted 9 flowers and 120 leaves on the bush. How many branches does the bush have?

solutions.title: Flowers first
solutions.body:
Each flower is on a branch with 4 leaves. 9 flowers → 9 such branches with $9 \times 4 = 36$ leaves.

The remaining $120 - 36 = 84$ leaves are on 7-leaf branches: $84 \div 7 = 12$ branches.

Total: $9 + 12 = 21$ branches.

**Answer: (B) 21**

solutions.title: Check the answer
solutions.body:
Try 21 branches: 9 have flowers (4 leaves each) and 12 have 7 leaves:
$9 \times 4 + 12 \times 7 = 36 + 84 = 120$ leaves ✓, and 9 flowers ✓.

**Answer: (B) 21**

prompt: Cynthia paints each region of the figure in a single colour: red, blue or yellow. Regions that touch each other must have different colours. In how many different ways can she colour the figure?

solutions.title: Each new region is forced
solutions.body:
Start from the outside:
- The outer ring, the top crescent just inside it, and the bottom crescent just inside it all touch each other. Give them three different colours: $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ ways.
- Going inwards, each next crescent touches the two regions just coloured (which have two different colours), so it must get the **third** colour — only 1 choice.
- The same happens all the way to the small circle in the middle.

So there are exactly $6$ ways.

**Answer: (E) 6**

solutions.title: Spot the repeating pattern
solutions.body:
Once you choose colours for the outer ring and the first two crescents, the colours repeat in the same order going inwards (for example red, blue, yellow, red, blue, yellow, …).

So the whole colouring depends only on the order of the three colours, and 3 colours can be put in order in $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ ways.

**Answer: (E) 6**

prompt: Five boxes contain 2, 3, 4, 7 and 15 balls respectively. Peter wants to move balls between the boxes so that every box has twice or half the number of balls of some other box. What is the smallest number of balls he must move?

solutions.title: Find a one-ball move
solutions.body:
Moving 0 balls doesn't work: 3 has no partner (no 6 and no 1.5).

Move **1 ball from the 15-box to the 3-box**: 2, 4, 4, 7, 14.
- 2 ↔ 4 (double) ✓
- both 4s ↔ 2 (half) ✓
- 7 ↔ 14 (double) ✓

Every box has a partner, so 1 ball is enough.

**Answer: (A) 1**

solutions.title: Look for pairs
solutions.body:
2 and 4 already pair up. 7 and 15 are almost a pair (7 and 14). And 3 is almost 4.

So take one ball from 15 (making 14) and give it to 3 (making 4): now 2–4–4 and 7–14 all work.

**Answer: (A) 1**

prompt: Two little mice, one white and one dark, leave at the same time towards the cheese along different paths, as shown in the picture, in which all the small squares are equal. The two arrive at the cheese at the same time. If the dark mouse runs 4.5 metres per second, how many metres per second does the white mouse run?

solutions.title: Count square sides
solutions.body:
Measure each path in square sides:
- White mouse: up 1, right 1, up 1, right 1 → **4** sides.
- Dark mouse: left 4, down 1, right 3, down 1, left 1, down 1, left 1 → **12** sides.

In the same time the dark mouse runs 3 times as far, so it is 3 times as fast. The white mouse runs $4.5 \div 3 = 1.5$ m/s.

**Answer: (B) 1.5**

solutions.title: Use a time
solutions.body:
The dark path is 12 sides and the white path is 4 sides. Suppose each side is 1.5 m: the dark mouse runs $12 \times 1.5 = 18$ m, taking $18 \div 4.5 = 4$ seconds. The white mouse runs $4 \times 1.5 = 6$ m in those 4 seconds: $6 \div 4 = 1.5$ m/s. (Any side length gives the same speed.)

**Answer: (B) 1.5**

prompt: The circles in the figure should be numbered from 0 to 10, each with a different number. The five sums of the three numbers on each diameter must all be odd. If one of these sums is the smallest possible, what is the largest possible value of one of the other sums?

solutions.title: Smallest sum first
solutions.body:
Every diameter uses the centre number plus two outer numbers.

The smallest possible sum of three different numbers is $0 + 1 + 2 = 3$, which is odd ✓. So the smallest sum is 3, made of 0, 1 and 2 — one of them in the centre.

To make another sum as big as possible, use the biggest numbers left, 9 and 10, plus the centre. So put **2** in the centre (and 0, 1 on one diameter): the sum $2 + 9 + 10 = 21$ is odd ✓.

Check the rest: centre 2 is even, so each diameter needs one odd and one even outer number: (0,1), (9,10), and the remaining 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 make (3,4), (5,6), (7,8) ✓.

**Answer: (E) 21**

solutions.title: Compare the centre choices
solutions.body:
The sum 3 can only be $0 + 1 + 2$, so the centre is 0, 1 or 2.

The largest other sum is at most centre $+ 9 + 10$:
- centre 0: $0 + 9 + 10 = 19$
- centre 1: $1 + 9 + 10 = 20$ (even, not allowed; best odd is $1 + 8 + 10 = 19$)
- centre 2: $2 + 9 + 10 = 21$ ✓ odd

So the largest possible is 21.

**Answer: (E) 21**

prompt: When Elisa the bat left her cave at night, the digital clock showed 10:20 (top picture). When she came back in the morning and hung herself upside down, she looked at the clock and saw 10:20 (bottom picture). How long did she stay out of the cave?

solutions.title: Turn the clock upside down
solutions.body:
Elisa sees the clock **upside down**. Turning "10:20" upside down reverses the order of the digits, and on a digital display the digits 1, 0 and 2 look the same upside down. So the real time was **02:01**.

She left at 10:20 at night and came back at 2:01 in the morning:
- 10:20 → 2:20 is 4 hours,
- 2:20 → 2:01 is 19 minutes back.

$4\text{ h} - 19\text{ min} = 3\text{ h } 41\text{ min}$.

**Answer: (D) 3h 41m**

solutions.title: Count up in steps
solutions.body:
Real times: left at 10:20 pm, returned at 2:01 am.
- 10:20 → 11:00: 40 min
- 11:00 → 2:00: 3 h
- 2:00 → 2:01: 1 min

Total: $3\text{ h} + 41\text{ min}$.

**Answer: (D) 3h 41m**

prompt: On a distant island, 2020 kangaroos holding hands form a large circle. Each kangaroo is either brown and always tells the truth, or grey and always lies. Each one of them says the same thing: "One of my neighbours is brown and the other is grey." How many brown kangaroos are in the circle?

solutions.title: Find the only possible pattern
solutions.body:
- A **brown** kangaroo tells the truth: one neighbour brown, one grey.
- A **grey** kangaroo lies: its two neighbours are the same colour (both brown or both grey).

Suppose there is a brown kangaroo. It has exactly one brown neighbour, so browns come in pairs: G **B B** G. The grey next to a pair has a brown on one side, so (lying) its other neighbour must also be brown. The pattern must repeat B B G B B G … all the way round — groups of 3.

But 2020 is not divisible by 3 ($2020 = 3 \times 673 + 1$), so this is impossible. Hence there are no brown kangaroos.

Check: all grey → each says "one brown, one grey", which is false ✓.

**Answer: (A) 0**

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
- 2020 brown: every neighbour is brown, so the statement would be false — but browns tell the truth ✗.
- 1010 brown alternating B G B G: a brown's neighbours are both grey — false ✗.
- 0 brown (all grey): each statement is false, and greys lie ✓.

The other numbers can't make a repeating B B G pattern around 2020 kangaroos either. Only 0 works.

**Answer: (A) 0**

prompt: Maria has exactly 9 white cubes, 9 light grey cubes and 9 dark grey cubes, all the same size. She glues all these cubes together to form a larger cube. Which of the cubes below is the one she made?

solutions.title: Only 8 cubes are hidden
solutions.body:
A $3 \times 3 \times 3$ cube has 27 small cubes. In each picture we see 19 of them; only $27 - 19 = 8$ are hidden. So **each colour must be visible at least once** (9 cubes of a colour can't all hide in 8 spots), and no colour can be visible more than 9 times.
- (B) and (E): no dark grey cube is visible ✗
- (D): no light grey cube is visible ✗
- (C): white is visible on 11 cubes ✗
- (A): 9 light grey, 9 dark grey and 1 white visible; the 8 hidden cubes are white ✓

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Count cube (A)
solutions.body:
Count the 19 visible cubes of (A): front face 9 cubes, 6 more on top, 4 more on the right side.
- Front: 4 light, 4 dark, 1 white (the centre)
- Top (back two rows): 3 light, 3 dark
- Right (the 4 new ones): 2 light, 2 dark

Light $= 9$, dark $= 9$, white $= 1$. The 8 hidden cubes are the other 8 whites — exactly 9 of each ✓.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: The figures show five paths, drawn with the thickest lines, between the points X and Y. Which of these paths is the longest?

solutions.title: Count arcs and straight pieces
solutions.body:
The circles have radii 1, 2 and 3 (Y is the centre). Every path is made of quarter-circle arcs and straight pieces of length 1. A quarter arc on circle 3 is 3 times as long as one on circle 1, so count arcs in "quarter-arcs of circle 1":
- (A): arcs 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 = **12**, plus 5 straight pieces
- (B): arcs 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 11, plus 5 straight pieces
- (C): arcs 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 9, plus 5 straight pieces
- (D): arcs 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 12, plus only 4 straight pieces
- (E): arcs 2 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 11, plus 5 straight pieces

(A) and (D) have the most arc length, and (A) has one more straight piece, so (A) is longest.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Compare (A) and (D) directly
solutions.body:
(A) and (D) go around the same circles in the same way: a quarter of the outer circle, a quarter of the middle circle, another quarter of the outer, another quarter of the middle, and then half of the small circle. But at the end, (A) still has to walk the straight piece from the small circle **into** Y, while (D)'s small half-circle already ends at its final point. That extra straight piece makes (A) longer. The others have clearly less arc length.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Mary numbered the faces of three cards from 1 to 6 (one number on each side of each card). Using these cards, she can make three-digit numbers, for example 135 or 234. But some numbers cannot be made, like 126. Which of the following numbers can **not** be made?

solutions.title: Work out the cards
solutions.body:
A number can be made only if its three digits are on three **different** cards.
- 135 works → 1, 3, 5 are on different cards.
- 234 works → 2, 3, 4 are on different cards.
- 126 doesn't work → two of 1, 2, 6 share a card.

Where is 3's partner? Not 1 or 5 (from 135), not 2 or 4 (from 234). So 3 is with **6**. Then from 126, 1 and 2 share a card: **{1, 2}**. The last card is **{4, 5}**.

So 4 and 5 are on the same card, and 245 can't be made.

**Answer: (D) 245**

solutions.title: Check each choice with the cards

prompt: Which of the following rigid pieces of wire, when copied, can make a closed shape without any crossings, with the two pieces joined at their ends?

solutions.title: Build it with piece (B)
solutions.body:
Piece (B) goes: up 2, right 1, down 1, right 1, up 1, right 1, down 1.

Take a second copy and turn it a **half turn** (upside down). Put it under the first piece so their ends touch: it goes down 2, left 1, up 1, left 1, down 1, left 1, up 1 — and meets the start of the first piece.

The two pieces together make a closed outline (like a square with notches) and never cross.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Why the others fail
solutions.body:
- (A), (C) and (D) are spirals: one end is trapped **inside** the curl, so a second copy can't reach it without crossing the wire.
- (E): if you turn a copy a half turn to join the ends, its middle corner lands exactly on the middle of the first piece, so they cross; other ways of joining don't close up.

Only (B) works.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Amelia sticks these six stickers on the faces of a cube: mouse, elephant, duck, ladybird, dog and fly. The figure shows the cube in two different positions. Which sticker is on the face opposite the duck?

solutions.title: Use the ladybird
solutions.body:
The ladybird appears in both pictures. Its neighbours are mouse and duck (picture 1) and fly and dog (picture 2). So these four go around the ladybird in a ring, and the **elephant** is opposite the ladybird.

So the duck is opposite one of mouse, dog or fly. Not the mouse — it is next to the duck in picture 1.

Now the order around the ladybird: in each picture go clockwise around the front corner. Picture 1: ladybird → mouse → duck. Picture 2: ladybird → dog → fly. So clockwise around the ladybird we have mouse then duck, and dog then fly: the ring is mouse, duck, dog, fly. Opposite faces are 2 apart in the ring: mouse–dog and **duck–fly**.

**Answer: (E) fly**

solutions.title: Build a paper cube
solutions.body:
Make a cube from paper (or use a box) and draw the six stickers to match the two pictures: put the ladybird on the front, the mouse on top and the duck on the right (picture 1). Then turn the cube until the fly is on top with the ladybird on the right (picture 2): the dog must be on the left. Now look at the face opposite the duck — it's the fly.

**Answer: (E) fly**

prompt: Beatriz and her five sisters are 2, 3, 5, 8, 10 and 17 years old. Beatriz writes these ages in the circles of the diagram so that the sum of the ages in the four corners of the square equals the sum of the ages in the four circles in the horizontal line. What is this sum?

choices.text: There is more than one possible value.

solutions.title: Cancel the shared circles
solutions.body:
The left and right corners of the square are also in the horizontal line. Take them away from both sums: the **top + bottom** circles must equal the **centre + far right** circles.

So we need two separate pairs of ages with the same sum. Checking pairs from 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 17, the only possibility is $3 + 10 = 5 + 8 = 13$.

The leftover ages, 2 and 17, go in the left and right corners. Sum of the corners: $13 + 2 + 17 = 32$.

**Answer: (D) 32**

solutions.title: Use the total
solutions.body:
All ages add up to $2 + 3 + 5 + 8 + 10 + 17 = 45$. If the equal pairs each sum to $p$, the four corners are one pair ($p$) plus the two shared circles ($45 - 2p$), so the sum is $45 - p$.

The only equal pairs are $3 + 10$ and $5 + 8$ ($p = 13$), so the sum is $45 - 13 = 32$. There is only one value.

**Answer: (D) 32**

prompt: Maria puts 4 litres of water in vase I, 3 litres in vase II and 4 litres in vase III, shown in the picture. Seen from the front, these three vases look the same size. Which of the following pictures could show the three vases seen from above?

solutions.title: Lower water means deeper vase
solutions.body:
From the front, all vases have the same width and height. So the amount of water depends on the water **height** and on the **depth** (front-to-back), which we only see from above.
- Vase III has 4 litres but the **lowest** water level → it must be the **deepest**.
- Vase I has 4 litres with a higher level than III → less deep than III.
- Vase II has only 3 litres and the **highest** level → the least deep.

From above: III longest, then I, then II shortest. That is picture (A).

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Compare in pairs
solutions.body:
- I and III hold the same 4 litres, but the water in III is lower, so III must be deeper than I. This rules out (B), (C) and (E).
- II holds less water than I but its level is higher, so II is narrower (less deep) than I. This rules out (D).

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Inside the grey square there are three white squares; the numbers inside them give their areas. The white squares have sides parallel to the sides of the grey square. If the area of the grey square is 81, what is the area of the grey part not covered by the white squares?

solutions.title: Find the side lengths
solutions.body:
- Grey square: area 81 → side 9.
- Top-left white square: area 9 → side 3.
- Bottom-right white square: area 4 → side 2.
- The middle white square fits between them corner to corner, so its side is $9 - 3 - 2 = 4$, area 16.

Grey area left: $81 - 9 - 16 - 4 = 52$.

**Answer: (C) 52**

solutions.title: Look along one side
solutions.body:
Walk along the bottom edge of the grey square from left to right: first 3 units under the small top-left square's width, then the middle square's width, then 2 units for the bottom-right square. These add to 9, so the middle square is 4 wide.

Uncovered area $= 81 - (3^2 + 4^2 + 2^2) = 81 - 29 = 52$.

**Answer: (C) 52**

prompt: John made a construction with wooden cubes of the same size, with the three views shown (front, right side, above), using as many cubes as possible. Ana, John's sister, wants to remove as many cubes as she can without changing these three views. At most, how many cubes can she remove?

solutions.title: Most cubes, then fewest cubes
solutions.body:
The view from above shows 12 occupied spots on a $4 \times 4$ grid. The front view gives the tallest stack in each column (3, 4, 3, 3) and the side view gives the tallest stack in each row (back to front: 4, 3, 2, 3).

**Most cubes:** make every stack as tall as both views allow (the smaller of its column and row heights). Adding up gives **34** cubes.

**Fewest cubes:** each of the 12 spots needs at least 1 cube, and we only need:
- one stack of 4 (for the column of height 4 and the back row),
- one stack of 3 in each of the other three columns (these can also take care of the rows of height 3),
- one stack of 2 in the row of height 2.

That is $4 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 15$ cubes in 5 stacks, plus 1 cube on each of the other 7 spots: $15 + 7 = 22$.

Ana can remove $34 - 22 = 12$ cubes.

**Answer: (B) 12**

solutions.title: Count what must stay
solutions.body:
Think about which stacks are really needed to make the outlines:
- The front view has 4 columns of heights 3, 4, 3, 3 → four tall stacks (one per column): 3 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 13 cubes, placed so that they also give the back row its 4 and two other rows their 3.
- The side view still needs a row of height 2 → one stack of 2.
- The top view needs every one of the 12 spots covered → the remaining 7 spots get 1 cube each.

$13 + 2 + 7 = 22$ cubes must stay. Since the full construction has 34 cubes, $34 - 22 = 12$ can go.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt: A panel is made of 4 circles. When Lucy touches a circle, that circle and the circles touching it change colour from white to black or from black to white, as shown in the picture. Starting with all circles white, what is the smallest number of circles Lucy must touch, one after another, so that all circles become black?

solutions.title: Touch every circle once
solutions.body:
Touching a circle flips it and its two neighbours (not the circle diagonally opposite).

Touch all 4 circles once each. Each circle gets flipped by itself and by its 2 neighbours: 3 flips — an odd number, so white → black ✓.

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: Why fewer doesn't work
solutions.body:
Touching the same circle twice undoes itself, so each circle is touched 0 or 1 times.
- 1 touch: flips 3 circles, one stays white ✗
- 2 touches on neighbouring circles: each of them is flipped twice (once by itself, once by the other) → back to white ✗
- 2 touches on diagonal circles: the other two circles are each flipped twice → white ✗
- 3 touches: the untouched circle is flipped by its 2 touched neighbours (twice → white) ✗

So 4 is the minimum.

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: Which set of weights below balances the third scale in the picture?

solutions.title: Swap shapes using the scales
solutions.body:
From the pictures:
- Scale 1: square + arrow = triangle + 2 circles
- Scale 2: 3 squares = triangle + circle
- Scale 3: 2 squares + arrow = ?

Scale 3 has one more square than scale 1, so it balances triangle + 2 circles + square.

Now replace "triangle + circle" by 3 squares (scale 2): triangle + 2 circles + square = (triangle + circle) + circle + square = 3 squares + circle + square = **1 circle + 4 squares**.

**Answer: (D) 1 circle and 4 squares**

solutions.title: Give the shapes weights
solutions.body:
Try circle = 1, square = 2. Scale 2: triangle + 1 = 6, so triangle = 5. Scale 1: 2 + arrow = 5 + 2, so arrow = 5.

Scale 3: $2 + 2 + 5 = 9$. Check the choices:
- (A) $4 \times 5 + 2 = 22$ ✗ (B) $15 + 1 = 16$ ✗ (C) $5 + 3 + 2 = 10$ ✗
- (D) $1 + 4 \times 2 = 9$ ✓ (E) $2 + 2 = 4$ ✗

**Answer: (D) 1 circle and 4 squares**

prompt: Ten people each order an ice cream: four vanilla, three chocolate, two lemon and one mango. As toppings they ask for four umbrellas, three cherries, two wafers and one chocolate gum — one topping on each ice cream. Since they don't want any two ice creams to be the same, which of the following combinations is possible?

solutions.title: Start with the biggest group
solutions.body:
- The 4 vanillas must all be different, so they get one of each topping: umbrella, cherry, wafer, **chocolate gum**. (So chocolate gum is on a vanilla.)
- Left: 3 umbrellas, 2 cherries, 1 wafer. The 3 chocolates need 3 different toppings: umbrella, cherry, **wafer**.
- Left: 2 umbrellas, 1 cherry. The 2 lemons need 2 different toppings: umbrella and **cherry**.
- Left: 1 umbrella for the mango.

So lemon with cherry happens, and all the other combinations are impossible.

**Answer: (E) Lemon with cherry**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
- Chocolate gum: there is only one, and the 4 different vanillas need all 4 toppings, so it is on a vanilla → (A) ✗.
- Both wafers end up on vanilla and chocolate → (C), (D) ✗.
- The mango gets the last umbrella → (B) ✗.

**Answer: (E) Lemon with cherry**

prompt: A three-digit number is called *balanced* if its middle digit is the average (arithmetic mean) of the other two digits. How many balanced numbers are divisible by 18?

solutions.title: Use the rules for 2 and 9
solutions.body:
Write the number as $a\,b\,c$ with $a + c = 2b$.
- Divisible by 9: digit sum $a + b + c = 3b$ must be a multiple of 9, so $b$ is 0, 3, 6 or 9.
- Divisible by 2: $c$ is even.

Check each $b$:
- $b = 0$: $a + c = 0$ — impossible ($a \ge 1$).
- $b = 3$: $a + c = 6$, $c$ even: 630, 432, 234.
- $b = 6$: $a + c = 12$, $c$ even: 864, 666, 468.
- $b = 9$: $a = c = 9$ → 999 is odd ✗.

Total: 6 numbers.

**Answer: (C) 6**

solutions.title: Check the list
solutions.body:
The six numbers are 234, 432, 630, 468, 666, 864.

Check one: $468 \div 18 = 26$ ✓, and 6 is the average of 4 and 8 ✓. All the others work the same way ($234 = 18 \times 13$, $432 = 18 \times 24$, $630 = 18 \times 35$, $666 = 18 \times 37$, $864 = 18 \times 48$).

**Answer: (C) 6**

prompt: Janaina bought three toys, spending all her money. For the first one she paid half of her money plus 1 real; for the second she paid half of what was left plus 2 reais; and for the third she paid half of what was left plus 3 reais. How much money did she have?

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
Start from the end, where she has 0.
- Third toy: half of what she had, plus 3, used everything. So the other half was 3: she had $6$ before the third toy.
- Second toy: after paying half plus 2 she had 6, so half of her money was $6 + 2 = 8$: she had $16$.
- First toy: after paying half plus 1 she had 16, so half was $16 + 1 = 17$: she had $34$.

**Answer: (A) 34 reais**

solutions.title: Check forwards
solutions.body:
Start with 34:
- First toy: $17 + 1 = 18$, left $16$.
- Second toy: $8 + 2 = 10$, left $6$.
- Third toy: $3 + 3 = 6$, left $0$ ✓

**Answer: (A) 34 reais**

prompt: Dirce built the sculpture shown by gluing together cubic boxes with sides of half a metre. Then she painted the sculpture, except for the bottom (the base it stands on), with a special paint sold in cans. Each can paints 4 square metres. How many cans of paint did she have to buy?

solutions.title: Count the painted squares
solutions.body:
The sculpture has 4 layers: $4 \times 4$, $3 \times 3$, $2 \times 2$ and $1 \times 1$ cubes.

- **From above:** you see a full $4 \times 4$ square of tops → 16 faces.
- **Sides:** each layer shows 4 sides; a layer of width $n$ shows $4n$ faces: $16 + 12 + 8 + 4 = 40$ faces.

Total: $16 + 40 = 56$ faces. Each face is $0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25$ m², so the area is $56 \div 4 = 14$ m².

$14 \div 4 = 3.5$, so she needs **4 cans**.

**Answer: (B) 4**

solutions.title: Look from each direction
solutions.body:
Look at the sculpture from the 5 directions that get paint (not from below):
- From above: a $4 \times 4$ square → 16 faces.
- From the front, back, left and right: each looks like a staircase of $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$ faces → $4 \times 10 = 40$.

56 faces of $\frac{1}{4}$ m² each = 14 m², which needs more than 3 cans of 4 m² ($12$ m²) but fits in 4 cans ($16$ m²).

**Answer: (B) 4**

prompt: Vania has a sheet of paper divided into nine equal squares. She folds the sheet as shown in the picture, first with horizontal folds and then with vertical folds, so that the coloured square ends up on top of the pile. She wants to write the numbers 1 to 9, one in each square, so that after folding they are in order from top to bottom, starting with 1 on top. On the open sheet (shown), which numbers should she write in place of $a$, $b$ and $c$?

solutions.title: Follow the layers
solutions.body:
**Horizontal folds** (zig-zag): the top row stays on top, the middle row goes under it, and the bottom row goes underneath. So we have a strip of 3 layers: top row, middle row, bottom row.

**Vertical folds** (zig-zag): the left column stays on top, the middle column folds under (and gets flipped over, so its 3 layers come in reverse order), then the right column comes last in normal order.

Pile from top to bottom:
1. left column: top, middle, bottom square → 1, 2, 3
2. middle column, reversed: bottom, middle, top square → 4, 5, 6
3. right column: top, middle, bottom square → 7, 8, 9

So $c$ (bottom-left) = 3, $b$ (centre) = 5, $a$ (top-right) = 7.

**Answer: (C) $a = 7$, $b = 5$, $c = 3$**

solutions.title: Use the centre and corners
solutions.body:
The centre square is in the middle row and middle column, so it ends up in the very middle of the pile: $b = 5$. That leaves (A), (C) and (D).

The bottom-left square is in the first column (on top after the vertical folds) and in the bottom row (third layer), so it is 3rd: $c = 3$. That leaves (A) and (C).

The top-right square is in the last column (last group: 7, 8, 9) and in the top row (first in that group), so $a = 7$.

**Answer: (C) $a = 7$, $b = 5$, $c = 3$**

prompt: The figure shows a map of some islands and the bridges connecting them. A navigator wants to visit each island exactly once. He started at Cang Island and wants to finish at Uru Island. He has just arrived at the black island in the centre of the map. In which direction must he go now to be able to complete his route? (On the compass, O = West and L = East.)

choices.text: There is more than one possible choice.

solutions.title: Islands with only two bridges
solutions.body:
An island with only 2 bridges (other than the start and finish) must use **both** of them: one to arrive, one to leave. Number rows 1–5 from the top and columns 1–5 from the left; the black island is (3,3).

- The islands along the top row and down the right side have only 2 bridges, so the route must start: Cang → along the top row → down the right side to (4,5) → (4,4).
- On the left, the islands with 2 bridges force a long chain: (4,3) – (4,2) – (3,2) – (2,2) – (2,1) – down the left side – along the bottom to (5,3). This uses up both bridges of (3,2), so the black island **can't go West**.
- Island (2,3) can only use its bridges to (2,4) and to the black island. And (2,4) can only use (2,3) and (3,4). So the route goes (4,4) → (3,4) → (2,4) → (2,3) → black island: it arrives from the **North**, and (3,4) to the **East** is already visited.

The only way left is **South**, to (4,3), and then along the chain to Uru.

**Answer: (C) South**

solutions.title: Write out a full route
solutions.body:
Number rows 1–5 from the top and columns 1–5 from the left. One complete route is:

Cang (1,1) → (1,2) → (1,3) → (1,4) → (1,5) → (2,5) → (3,5) → (4,5) → (4,4) → (3,4) → (2,4) → (2,3) → **black (3,3)** → **(4,3)** → (4,2) → (3,2) → (2,2) → (2,1) → (3,1) → (4,1) → (5,1) → (5,2) → (5,3) → (5,4) → Uru (5,5).

From the black island the route goes to (4,3), which is **south**. North (2,3) and East (3,4) have already been visited, and West (3,2) has to be passed through between (2,2) and (4,2), so it can't be entered from the black island.

**Answer: (C) South**
